queue.tree_name: Elku Linden of Valdemārpils (Linden of Sacrifice)
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 8.65 metres round near the ground and hollow, with parts of the tree held by cables and cement. It stands in the Sasmaka manor park and is the one obvious giant there.
queue.story:
Inside the hollow trunk of the thickest lime in the Baltic states, the wood has grown into shapes that visitors read as owls, hedgehogs, turtles and snakes.

The Elku linden stands in the old Sasmaka manor park on the edge of Valdemārpils. In 2025 Talsi municipality measured it at 8.65 metres round, taken low, at 30 centimetres above the ground, with a height of 25 metres and a crown covering some 320 square metres.

Its name is its oldest story. Elku means idols, or sacrifice, and tradition says this was once a tree where offerings were made. Folklore and Latvia's heritage site senvietas.lv give it 400 to 500 years. The municipality disagrees: measurements in 2023 found it growing about 3.5
queue.name: Elku Linden of Valdemārpils (Linden of Sacrifice)
queue.worth: closes a gap: this tree has no photograph at all

queue.tree_name: Dab Mieszko I (King Mieszko I's Oak)
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by steel cables holding up its one surviving thick branch and a cavity filled with brick and cement. It stands at the edge of Natolin Forest, on Nowoursynowska Street.
queue.story: Warsaw's oldest tree survived six centuries of Polish history only to be set on fire by a person, not a storm, in June 2019. The oak, named for Poland's first recorded ruler though it began growing roughly two and a half centuries after his death around 992, stands at the edge of Natolin Forest on the city's southern edge, one of the last fragments of the wild Mazovian woodland that once covered this ground before Warsaw existed at all. queue.name: Dab Mieszko I (King Mieszko I's Oak)

queue.tree_name: The Pear-Barked Beech
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the graft line at about two metres up, rough pear bark below and smooth grey beech bark above. It stands in York Museum Gardens, near the ruins of St Mary's Abbey.
queue.story: Halfway up the trunk of this beech, at almost exactly two metres, the bark changes: rough and fissured like a pear tree's below the line, smooth and grey like an ordinary beech's above it. That is because it is not one tree but two, grafted together when the Yorkshire Philosophical Society was filling York Museum Gardens with botanical curiosities, and the join has held long enough that the tree now stands nineteen metres tall with a trunk almost three metres round, one of Yorkshire's six Tree Register champions inside these ten acres. Pear bark grafted onto beech rootstock, or the other way round (records from the planting era do not say which), was the kind of horticultural party trick Vic
queue.name: The Pear-Barked Beech

queue.tree_name: The Copper Beech of the Badenburg
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by leaves that open bright translucent red in late April and darken toward black by August, standing about 25 metres south of the Badenburg bathing pavilion. It stands in Schlosspark Nymphenburg.
queue.story: Every copper beech in Europe descends from an accident. The purple leaf is a mutation that appears rarely and at random in wild green beech forests, and every ornamental one since has been propagated by gardeners who found the freak worth keeping. This one stands about 25 metres south of the Badenburg, the bathing pavilion Joseph Effner built for Elector Max Emanuel between 1718 and 1721 around what is generally reckoned the first heated indoor pool built in Europe since Roman times. queue.tree_name: The Gomero de la Recoleta
queue.recognise: The huge fig with a car-parts sculpture of Atlas appearing to hold up one long branch, a few metres from the Recoleta Cemetery gate.
queue.story: One branch of this fig reaches thirty metres out from the trunk and is over a metre thick where it leaves it. Since 2014 a sculpture of Atlas, welded from car parts by the Uruguayan artist Joaquin Arbiza Brianza, has stood underneath it appearing to take the weight. The city government calls this the oldest tree in Buenos Aires, and nobody agrees on how it got here. One account has the Recoleto friars planting it around 1718. Another credits the agronomist Martin Jose de Altolaguirre, who kept an orchard of exotic species on this ground around 1781. queue.tree_name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the Amalienburg
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by leaves shredded into narrow ribbons, with the odd branch reverting to ordinary broad beech leaves, standing alone at a path fork. It stands about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, Schlosspark Nymphenburg.
queue.story: No fern-leaved beech anywhere is much more than two centuries old, because the tree did not exist before about 1804. It is a cultivated form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow ribbons, and it cannot be relied on to come true from seed, so every one of them has been grafted or struck from cuttings taken off another. That gives this specimen an unusually hard ceiling on its age, which is useful in a park where almost nothing else has a date. It stands alone at a fork in the path about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, the rococo hunting lodge Francois de Cuvillies built in the 1730s, with a small metal plate on the trunk marking it as a natural monument. queue.tree_name: The Cardón of the Expo
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its bundle of tall, ribbed green columns rising from one trunk, held by rusty steel props in a gravel bed. It stands on the paved corner of Calle Tomás Alva Edison and Calle Johannes Kepler.
queue.story:
Mexico flew this cactus to Seville. It was the country's gift to Spain for Expo '92, picked from the most slender giants in the Valle de los Gigantes in Baja California, and taking it turned into a political row. Digging started on 14 December 1991. People in the area protested, the dispute reached the state congress, and work stopped in January before resuming a month later. The fuss left something behind, and the valley was declared a sanctuary for its cardones and is protected today.

The cactus came out of the ground with about ten metres of roots, in a steel cage lifted by three cranes, rode a thirty-wheel trailer to Hermosillo and flew via Miami, landing in Seville on 23 March 1992. Se

queue.tree_name: The Leaning Lime of the Badenburger See
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk leaning hard over the water with its heaviest limbs thrown sideways rather than up, a bench underneath facing the Monopteros. It stands on the Badenburger See shore, Schlosspark Nymphenburg.
queue.story: Munich protects this lime, in law, for being strange looking. The reason recorded in the city's natural monument ordinance is bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, together with a striking appearance, which is an unusually candid thing for a protection statute to say about a tree. It earns it. The trunk leans hard out over the Badenburger See and the whole crown follows, throwing its heaviest limbs sideways across the water rather than upward, so the tree reads as a single long gesture toward the lake. queue.name: The Leaning Lime of the Badenburger See

queue.tree_name: The Fortingall Yew
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its several separate stems, once a single trunk that split apart from the 1770s onward, now ringed by a low wall built in 1785 to stop souvenir-taking. It stands inside Fortingall churchyard.
queue.story:
In 2015 a tree that had been male for as long as anyone had recorded it grew berries on a single branch. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh reported the change, and beyond the novelty it was proof that the Fortingall Yew is a working organism rather than a standing relic.

Its age is genuinely disputed and always will be. Forestry and Land Scotland says 5,000 years. Bevan-Jones, the standard academic reference on ancient yews, gives 2,000 to 3,000 and allows that the tree may only date from a post-Roman Christian site here, which would make it around 1,500. Nobody can settle it, because the heartwood rotted out centuries ago and there are no rings left to count.

queue.tree_name: The Cut-Leaved Hornbeam
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a hollow trunk and a low, curling canopy that brushes the grass, with finely cut, deeply serrated leaves. It stands among York Museum Gardens' cluster of champion trees.
queue.story: The Cut-Leaved Hornbeam's trunk is hollow, its canopy hangs low enough to brush the grass, and the whole tree curls into itself rather than growing straight up, more contorted shrub than the neat street tree hornbeams usually become. That shape earned it a place on the Tree Register's list of Yorkshire county champions, the largest recorded example of its cultivar in the county. queue.tree_name: The Bromley Oak
queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the lone veteran oak on the grass beside the road. It stands beside Kentish Way, on the edge of The Glades shopping centre grounds.
queue.story:
When Bromley built The Glades shopping centre in the 1980s, this oak was reprieved. It now stands beside Kentish Way, a veteran on the grass at the edge of a mall that opened in 1991.

It was here long before any of that. The Bromley Civic Society says the oak first stood on the corner of the grounds of Bromley Lodge, where they met Love Lane.

How long it has stood there is disputed. The Civic Society calls it over 500 years old; the 2010 Time Out guide to the Great Trees of London says about 400. queue.tree_name: The Great Cedar of Kasuga Taisha
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the second tree growing from its base, reaching toward the neighbouring hall through a hole cut in the roof. It stands beside the Naoraiden, near Kasuga Taisha's inner gate.
queue.story: There is a picture scroll, donated to this shrine in 1309, in which this cedar appears as a sapling. Seven centuries later it is roughly eight metres around and twenty-five tall, standing beside the hall where offerings are shared after the rituals, and the sapling in the painting is the same organism. Almost no ancient tree anywhere can be checked against its own portrait as a young plant. The better story is what grows out of its base. A second tree, a shinpaku, took root there and grew toward the neighbouring hall, and rather than cut it back somebody cut a hole in the roof and let it through. The hall still has the hole. Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768 for the deity of the Fujiwara clan
queue.name: The Great Cedar of Kasuga Taisha

queue.tree_name: The Witch Tree of Fanal
queue.recognise: A hard-twisted trunk with limbs reading as outstretched arms under a coat of moss. Nothing on the ground names it and there is no path to it, so the pin marks the grove rather than the tree.
queue.story:
The grove these trees belong to was already standing when the Portuguese found Madeira uninhabited in 1419. Fanal is a protected 20-hectare nucleus of til, Ocotea foetens, on the Paul da Serra plateau inside the UNESCO laurel forest, and the island's register dates it only as centenas de anos, hundreds of years, referencing a stand that predates settlement. The eight trunks the surveyors measured run from 0.68 to 2.28 metres round.

queue.tree_name: The Weeping Beech of Helfenberg Park
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the concrete filling a hole in the trunk at about 1.5 metres, and by the fallen trunk of its twin, uprooted in 2015, left lying in the grass. It stands in the park south of the Helfenberg manor house.
queue.story:
Of the two weeping beeches this park was protected for, one now lies on the grass. Storm Niklas pulled the larger and more imposing of the pair out of the ground on 31 March 2015. Dresden left the fallen tree where it fell, as habitat for wildlife, and planted a young one into its root zone.

The survivor is the one to walk to, and it has had the harder life. In 1985 a hole in its trunk, a metre and a half up, was filled with concrete, and it has since lost a large limb. The pair were described as about 20 metres tall with crowns some 25 metres across, the biggest and gnarliest weeping beeches in the area. Measurements disagree. queue.tree_name: The Ficus of the Orto Botanico
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the 44 secondary trunks dropping from the branches and thickening into columns where they reach the ground, under a crown of some 3,000 square metres. It stands inside the ticketed Orto Botanico.
queue.story: The most famous fig tree in Palermo is not the one in Piazza Marina, it is that tree's parent. Planted in the Orto Botanico in 1845, this Ficus macrophylla has spent 180 years building a canopy now measured at roughly 3,000 square metres, reportedly the largest crown of any tree in Europe, spread across 44 secondary trunks that grow down from the branches as aerial roots and thicken into full columns once they reach the ground. In 2023 it placed fourth in the European Tree of the Year contest after winning Italy's own national vote first, on the strength of more than 10,000 European votes. queue.tree_name: The Kaditzer Linde
queue.recognise: Not a trunk but a standing half shell, wide open on one side, with a curved wooden bench built around its foot and steel cables running up into the crown. A war memorial with a stone eagle stands a few metres away.
queue.story:
Half of this tree burned in 1818 and what holds the other half up is its own roots.

A fire that year took eighteen farms, thirty barns and the parsonage of Kaditz, and the lime beside the church went with them. The side facing the parsonage died outright. What survived is a half shell of trunk, and the city's sign on it explains the trick that kept the thing alive. The stems standing inside the hollow are former roots that turned into supports.

Dresden calls it the oldest tree in the city and will not put a number on it. The sign says many centuries old, then adds a thousand years with a question mark after it. Nothing can be counted, because the trunk has been damaged too often for rings
queue.name: The Kaditzer Linde
